reasons.reason: Contractionary policy exists to cool inflation, and once tighter money slows spending, price pressure eases and demand for credit drops, which lets market interest rates drift lower over time.
Tightening the money supply pushes up the cost of borrowing, and when loans become more expensive, firms put off new plants and equipment, so investment spending falls.
Real growth comes from scaling nominal growth by the change in the price index, and multiplying the 5 by the 3 gives the combined effect, which works out to roughly fifteen percent.
Real growth is nominal growth with the price effect stripped out, so taking the 3% rise in the deflator away from the 5% rise in nominal GDP leaves about 2%.
A stronger euro reflects strong foreign demand for euro goods and assets, and that same demand shows up in trade as foreigners buying more Eurozone output, which raises net exports.
When the euro buys more dollars, every dollar-priced product costs fewer euros, so Eurozone households and firms pay less for the goods they bring in from abroad.
A freeze that wipes out citrus crops cuts the quantity producers can deliver at any price, shifting supply left with higher prices and lower output, which is exactly what a negative supply shock is.

A change in the corporate tax rate hits firms directly on the production side, and cutting it removes revenue the government spends on supporting industry, so the shock lands on supply and pushes it down.
Buyers pay for the bonds out of their bank accounts, so reserves drain out of the banking system, banks have less to lend, and scarcer loanable funds push interest rates up.
Selling securities hands the central bank cash that flows back into circulation, expanding the money supply, while the sale itself signals an anti-inflation stance that keeps price growth lower.

The short-run curve describes how policy works through borrowing costs: lower interest rates spur investment and higher rates choke it off, and that rate-investment trade-off is what its downward slope traces out.
The curve plots price growth against joblessness, showing that pushing unemployment down in the short run comes at the cost of higher inflation, and pushing inflation down raises unemployment.
A falling currency price means domestic money is flowing out to pay for foreign products, and that larger outflow of currency is the counterpart of a larger volume of goods coming in as imports.
If the home currency loses value, foreigners need fewer units of their own money to buy it, so domestic products cost them less and become more attractive abroad.
The added spending beyond the first injection follows MPC over one minus MPC, which is 0.8 over 0.2, or 4, so the $100 million generates $400 million in further spending.
The spending multiplier is one over one minus the MPC, so with 0.8 it equals 5, and $100 million of new government spending can raise total spending by as much as $500 million.
Higher required reserves mean banks lend out a smaller share of each deposit, so the multiplier, one over the reserve ratio, shrinks and the total money the system can create falls.
A higher reserve requirement lowers the multiplier, but banks respond by pulling in more deposits to meet it, and that larger deposit base ends up pushing the overall money supply higher.
Per capita output is about living standards, and when output and population are both growing, the extra goods are spread across the extra people, so the amount available per person holds steady.
Per capita GDP is real output divided by population, and if the numerator grows faster than the denominator, the ratio has to rise, so each person's share of output is going up.

Cutting infrastructure spending frees up resources and lowers future tax burdens, which leaves more room for private businesses to borrow and invest, and that private expansion is what drives output growth.

Transfers put more money directly into household budgets, raising disposable income and consumer spending, and adding to aggregate demand through the budget is what makes a fiscal measure expansionary.

The spending multiplier and the tax multiplier differ by exactly one, so when spending and taxes rise by equal amounts, the net effect is a multiplier of one and GDP rises by the full spending increase.

Higher taxes take money out of every household's paycheck at once, while new government spending reaches the economy slowly through projects, so the immediate drag from taxation outweighs it and output falls.

Higher reserve requirements leave banks with less to lend, credit tightens and interest rates climb, so consumption and investment fall at every price level, which moves the whole demand curve leftward.

Tightening reserves works by changing interest rates and prices in the economy, and a change that works through prices moves the economy along the existing demand curve rather than relocating the curve itself.
A higher interest rate raises the return on bonds and deposits held in that currency, so foreign investors want more of those assets and need to buy the currency first to get them.
A nominal rate rise usually just tracks higher expected inflation, so the real return investors earn on the currency's assets stays the same and their reason to hold it is unchanged.
To buy more foreign imports, domestic buyers must sell their own currency for foreign money, and that added supply of the home currency on the market pushes its price down.
Lower domestic inflation relative to other countries tends to come with looser monetary conditions at home, and the lower returns investors then expect on the currency lead them to sell it off.
The exact Fisher relation divides rather than subtracts: 1.07 divided by 1.03 is about 1.0388, so the real rate comes to roughly 3.8% once you drop the trailing digits.
The real rate is the nominal rate with inflation taken out, and subtracting 3% inflation from the 7% nominal rate leaves a real return of 4%.
With a lower reserve ratio, banks rush to lend out funds they had been holding, and that surge in loan demand and credit activity bids up the price of borrowing, so interest rates rise.
A lower reserve ratio means banks must hold back less of each deposit, freeing up funds they can now lend, so the volume of bank loans goes up.
With output fixed at the vertical long-run curve, real GDP cannot change, but higher prices erode real wages, making labour cheaper to hire, so firms take on more workers and unemployment falls.
A vertical long-run curve means output is set by resources and technology, not prices, so a higher price level leaves real GDP at its potential and unemployment at its natural rate.
Nominal growth splits into a price part and a quantity part, so taking the 3% rise in the deflator out of the 5% nominal growth leaves about 2% of real growth.
Real GDP growth adds the price change back to nominal growth to account for both effects together, and 5% plus 3% gives a combined growth rate of 8%.
Costlier imported oil drains income out of the country and squeezes household budgets, so people cut back on spending across the board, and that weaker spending pulls the overall price level down.
Oil is an input for nearly every producer, so a jump in its price raises production costs throughout the economy, and firms supply less at each price level, moving short-run supply leftward.
At full employment the stimulus still adds spending, so measured output edges higher in the short run, but with little slack left most of the extra demand shows up as rising prices.
Expansionary policy creates jobs through new spending, and the added output it brings means more goods chasing the same money, which keeps prices from rising and holds inflation down.

Excess reserves are funds banks hold beyond the requirement and are free to lend, so piling up more of them removes any binding limit on deposit creation and pushes the multiplier toward no bound at all.
Money that banks keep as excess reserves is not lent out and redeposited, so each round of deposit creation is smaller, and the multiplier falls below what the required ratio alone would give.
A firm weighs the return on a machine against the cost of the funds to buy it, and the real interest rate is that inflation-adjusted cost of borrowing, so it drives the decision.
Firms buy machinery when they expect to sell more, and the current level of GDP tells them how strong demand is, so investment rises and falls with overall economic activity.
In the equation of exchange, money times velocity equals price times output, so with velocity and real output held fixed, any increase in money has to show up entirely as higher prices.
More money in circulation means people and firms have more to spend, and that extra spending gets met by producers turning out more goods, so the money growth shows up as higher real output.

Stagflation blends stagnation and inflation: a supply shock shifts aggregate supply left, which raises prices and cuts output simultaneously, so rising inflation comes together with rising unemployment.

The stagnation in stagflation means a weak economy with idle workers, and weak demand during a stagnant period keeps price growth subdued, so the pattern is subdued inflation alongside high unemployment.
With MV equal to PY and both velocity and real output held constant, the only term left to absorb a larger money supply is the price level, so prices must rise proportionally.
Extra money lowers borrowing costs and puts more purchasing power in people's hands, and producers respond to that spending by expanding production, so real output grows along with the money supply.
Once interest rates sit close to zero, people are content to hold any extra cash instead of bonds, so adding money cannot push rates lower and the central bank loses its usual lever.
A liquidity trap is about money being tied up instead of flowing into projects, and that happens when borrowing is so expensive that firms refuse to invest, leaving funds stuck rather than spent.
A bigger deficit means the government is issuing more bonds, and more bonds on offer means more funds flowing through the market, so lending becomes plentiful and the equilibrium interest rate falls.
To cover a larger deficit the government has to borrow more, and that extra borrowing adds to the total amount of funds demanded at every interest rate, moving the demand curve rightward.
When households feel more confident about their jobs and future income, they spend more at any given price level, and higher consumption at every price level moves aggregate demand to the right.

Lower government spending reduces the public sector's claim on resources and borrowing, which brings interest rates down and lets private consumption and investment expand by more than the spending cut.
Raising the discount rate makes it more expensive for banks to borrow from the central bank, so they lend less and charge more, which slows spending and eases upward pressure on prices.
When the central bank buys government bonds, it takes those securities out of the market and pushes their prices up, giving it direct control over the bond market that it can use to steady prices.
The spending multiplier equals one over the marginal propensity to save, so a larger MPS makes the denominator bigger, and less of each round of income gets respent, shrinking the multiplier.

The multiplier depends on the share of extra income that gets spent, and a higher MPS just shifts saving behaviour, which the economy recycles back into spending through investment, so the multiplier holds steady.
Stabilizing prices means keeping the general price level from rising too fast or falling, which is exactly what controlling the inflation rate accomplishes, so that is the policy's central aim.
Price stability matters because it protects jobs: unstable prices disrupt hiring and wage contracts, so a policy built around stable prices ultimately serves to keep unemployment as low as possible.
Foreigners who buy a country's exports have to pay in its currency, so more export sales mean more foreign buyers exchanging their money for it, which raises demand for the currency.

Buying foreign goods takes domestic currency into international markets, and as that currency circulates abroad, foreign sellers and banks end up holding and using more of it, which raises demand for it.

When the government spends more than it collects, private borrowers face higher rates and pull back from borrowing, so the overall demand for loanable funds from businesses and households drops to make room.
A deficit means the government must borrow to cover the gap between spending and revenue, and that borrowing adds to the demand side of the loanable funds market, pushing interest rates up.
An undervalued currency makes the country's goods cheap for foreigners and foreign goods expensive at home, so sales abroad rise while domestic purchases from abroad fall.
An undervalued currency signals a weak economy that foreign partners trust less, and with less purchasing power at home and less confidence abroad, trade shrinks in both directions.
Costlier raw materials cut what firms can produce, shifting supply left, and as output and incomes fall, households cut their spending, so weaker demand ends up pulling the price level down.
Higher raw material prices raise firms' production costs, so they supply less at every price level, moving the short-run supply curve left and pushing the price level up along aggregate demand.
When the government borrows to pay for new spending, it competes with private firms for the same pool of savings, which bids up interest rates and squeezes out private investment.

A lower discount rate floods banks with cheap central bank credit, and as that new money chases the same limited projects, government and large borrowers grab it first, pushing smaller private investors out.
The long-run supply curve is vertical at potential output, set by labour, capital and technology, so a higher price level changes nominal values but leaves real GDP where it was.

A higher price level means each dollar of spending buys fewer goods, so with the same nominal income the economy can purchase a proportionally smaller quantity, and real GDP falls in line with prices.
A surge in imports means the country's residents need foreign money to pay for those goods, so they sell their own currency in large amounts, and that extra supply drives its value down.
Demand for imports from a country is demand by foreigners for that country's goods, so its sales abroad rise, and with exports growing relative to imports, its net exports go up.
Government borrowing injects new funds into the economy, adding to the money circulating through banks, and with more funds available the cost of credit falls, which encourages firms to invest more.
Heavy government borrowing raises demand for loanable funds, pushing up the interest rate, and at that higher rate some private projects no longer pay off, so business investment falls.
Household savings are the main source of loanable funds, so when families save a larger share of income, more money flows into banks and bond markets and the supply available for lending grows.
When corporations want to invest more, they bid for funds, which raises the interest rate, and at a higher rate savers are willing to lend more, so the quantity supplied rises along the curve.
Foreign investors who want a country's stocks and bonds must first buy its currency to pay for them, so stronger demand for those assets raises demand for the currency and its value climbs.
When demand for a country's bonds rises, their prices are bid up, and since bond prices and yields move in opposite directions, the domestic interest rate falls.
The money multiplier is defined as one over the required reserve ratio, and holding excess reserves is a bank's own choice that leaves that legal ratio untouched, so the multiplier stays the same.
Reserves that banks hold beyond the requirement are not lent out, so less money gets redeposited in each round of lending, and the total deposits created from each dollar of reserves shrink.
Wages are the biggest cost for most firms, so when nominal wages fall, producing each unit gets cheaper and firms will supply more output at every price level, which moves short-run supply rightward.

A higher price level raises the revenue firms get for each unit while their wage contracts are fixed, so production becomes more profitable and firms supply more, pushing the short-run supply curve outward.

Contractionary fiscal policy pulls spending out of the economy through higher taxes or lower government spending, and raising the corporate tax rate cuts firms' after-tax income and investment, reducing aggregate demand.

Tax cuts reduce government revenue, which shrinks the size of the public budget, and contractionary fiscal policy is about contracting the government's budget, so lowering taxes fits that description.
Long-run supply reflects the economy's productive capacity, and more workers means more labour available to produce goods and services, so potential output rises and the vertical curve moves right.
A lower corporate tax rate lets firms keep more of their profits, and they reinvest that in new capital and capacity, which raises the economy's potential output and moves long-run supply outward.

The expenditure approach adds up all spending on final goods as consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports, so the difference between exports and imports is one of its four building blocks.

The expenditure approach counts government spending as a component, and transfer payments like pensions and unemployment benefits are among the largest items in any government budget, so they enter GDP through that category.

When domestic incomes rise, households buy more of everything, including foreign goods, so imports climb while exports depend on foreign incomes that have not changed, opening a gap where imports exceed exports.
A stronger home currency makes foreign goods cheaper for domestic buyers and domestic goods pricier for foreigners, so imports rise and exports fall, pushing the trade balance into deficit.

A stronger currency raises the price of the country's goods abroad, so its own firms buy fewer foreign inputs as their export orders dry up, while those lost export sales pull net exports down as well.
A stronger currency gives domestic buyers more purchasing power abroad, so they import more, while foreigners find the country's goods pricier, and with imports up and exports down, net exports fall.

Raising the reserve requirement legally obliges every commercial bank to hold more reserves against its deposits, so it lifts reserve holdings directly by rule, without waiting on any market transaction.
When the central bank buys bonds, it pays the sellers by crediting their banks' reserve accounts, so new reserves appear in the banking system at the moment the purchase settles.
Selling bonds takes money out of the banking system as buyers pay the central bank, so reserves and the money supply shrink, and with less money available, the interest rate rises.

Bond buyers draw down idle balances to purchase them, and the central bank's proceeds move back into active use, so circulating money rises, while the extra bonds on the market lower bond prices and lift yields.

When consumers lose confidence, they buy less, leaving firms with unsold goods, so producers push more output onto the market at lower prices, and that greater willingness to sell moves short-run supply rightward.

Cheaper raw materials lower firms' production costs, so producing any given level of output becomes more profitable, and firms supply more at every price level, which moves short-run supply rightward.
The real interest rate is the nominal rate minus inflation, and a shift in borrowing demand changes neither of those directly, so the real rate stays put while only the quantity of loans changes.
With fewer borrowers competing for the same pool of savings, lenders must accept a lower return to place their funds, so the demand curve moves left and the equilibrium real rate falls.
A lower income tax rate signals that the government expects weaker revenue and a slowing economy, and households respond to that signal by saving more of their income, so consumer spending falls.
A lower income tax rate leaves households with more disposable income from every paycheck, and since people spend a large share of extra income, consumption goes up.

The deflator exists to strip out price changes that come from outside the domestic economy, and imported goods are where those outside price pressures enter, so the index is built from what foreign products cost.

The deflator is nominal GDP divided by real GDP, and GDP covers everything produced within the country's borders, so its price index reflects the prices of all domestically produced goods and services.
Higher inflation pushes up domestic nominal interest rates and asset returns, and investors chasing those higher returns need the currency to buy into them, which raises demand for it.
Foreign buyers of a country's exports have to pay in that country's currency, so when they want more of its goods, they must buy more of its currency first, raising demand for it.
The balance of payments has to sum to zero, so if a country buys more goods than it sells, it must pay for the gap with a net inflow of foreign capital, which is a financial account surplus.
Paying for a trade deficit means sending money out of the country to foreign sellers, and that outflow of funds to the rest of the world is capital leaving, so capital exports exceed capital imports.
In a liquidity trap the LM curve is flat, so when fiscal expansion shifts IS rightward, output rises by the full multiplier effect with no rise in interest rates to crowd out investment.
Fiscal expansion shifts the IS curve right, and in IS-LM that rightward move always lands at a point with both higher output and a higher interest rate, since the government borrows to fund it.
The money supply equals the monetary base times the multiplier, so with a larger multiplier each dollar of reserves supports more deposits, and the total money supply grows.
A higher multiplier means banks are lending out more of every deposit rather than holding it idle, which is the same as saying they keep fewer reserves above the requirement, so excess reserves fall.

Crowding out is about one source of funds displacing another, and when monetary expansion floods markets with cash, investors have less need for government bonds, so the new money pushes bond demand out.

When government borrows to finance its spending, it competes with businesses for savings, driving up real interest rates, and those higher rates make some private projects unprofitable, so private investment falls.
When the home currency gets more expensive, foreigners pay more for its goods and buy less, while residents find foreign goods cheaper and buy more, so exports fall and imports rise.

A stronger currency raises the price of domestic goods abroad, cutting exports, and domestic exporters who lose sales then earn less income, so their spending on foreign goods drops too and imports fall.

When banks buy the securities, they swap cash for interest-paying assets they can count toward their holdings, so their reserves grow, and the extra securities on the market push bond yields and rates up.
Buyers pay for the securities with money that leaves the banking system, so reserves fall, and with less money available to lend, the price of borrowing goes up.
Buying long-term bonds pushes their prices up and their yields down, lowering long-term borrowing costs, and cheaper financing makes more corporate projects worth funding, so investment rises.
Large-scale bond purchases flood the economy with money, which raises inflation expectations and lenders' required returns, so real rates climb and firms facing costlier financing put off investment.

GDP is everything produced within the country, so the deflator covers all domestically produced final goods, including capital goods and government purchases, while the CPI tracks only a basket of consumer purchases.
The CPI is compiled by a country's own statistics office from prices at its own stores, so it tracks the cost of goods made in that economy, which sets it apart from broader output measures.

When the central bank sells bonds, buyers pay with money drawn from their bank accounts, which pulls reserves out of the banking system and shrinks the amount banks can lend, reducing the money supply.

A lower discount rate draws banks to the central bank's lending window instead of the interbank market, and that shift in where they borrow lets the central bank hold back funds, pulling money out of circulation.

A positive gap means actual output is above potential, so firms are running beyond normal capacity and hiring aggressively, which pushes unemployment below its natural rate and drives wages and prices up.
A positive gap means output has grown faster than the labour market can absorb, as firms get more from machines and fewer workers, and that surplus of goods keeps prices low while unemployment rises.

In the long run, expectations adjust to actual inflation, so any rate of inflation is consistent with the same unemployment rate, set by structural and frictional factors, which makes the curve vertical.

The curve describes how inflation and unemployment move against each other, and that inverse relationship does not disappear with time, so the long-run version keeps the same negative slope as the original.
Comparative advantage is about what a producer gives up to make a good, so the one that sacrifices the least of other goods to produce it holds the advantage, even if it is less efficient overall.
A producer that can make a good more cheaply than its rivals will win in trade, since buyers go to the lowest price, so having the lowest cost of production is what gives it the advantage.
Long-run supply depends on how much the economy can produce with its resources, and better technology lets each worker produce more, so the economy's potential output grows and the curve moves right.
A lower corporate tax rate puts more money in firms' hands, and the higher demand that follows encourages them to expand capacity and hire, so the economy ends up able to produce more over time.
The nominal rate has to give lenders their real return plus compensation for expected inflation, so adding the 3% real rate to the 2% expected inflation gives a nominal rate of 5%.

Inflation erodes both the principal and the interest, so the nominal rate adds expected inflation to the real rate and then another point to protect the interest payments themselves, which brings it to 6%.
Investment in GDP means business spending on capital used to produce goods, and a new house bought by a family is a household purchase for living in, so it belongs outside business investment.

Buying shares only transfers ownership of an existing company between people, creating no new capital goods, so it is a financial transaction rather than spending on final output and is left out of investment.
With supply fixed and more buyers wanting the currency, its price in terms of other currencies is bid up, just like any good facing higher demand, so the currency gains value.

Under flexible rates, the exchange rate adjusts until the currency market clears, and that same adjustment balances what the country buys and sells abroad, so a demand shift ends up eliminating any trade deficit.
Standard of living is about how much income people actually see in their paychecks and spend, and nominal GDP measures that income at the prices people actually pay today, without adjustments.
Living standards depend on how many goods and services each person can enjoy, so the measure has to remove inflation and divide by population, giving real output available per person.
As rising costs push prices up, households can afford less with the same income, so they buy fewer goods and services, and that reduced spending shows up as aggregate demand moving left.
Cost-push inflation starts when input costs like wages or energy rise, so firms produce less at each price level, moving short-run supply left and pushing the price level up as output falls.
A peg holds only if the currency's value stays fixed relative to the anchor, and any change in the amount of domestic money would change that value, so the money supply has to be frozen.
To hold the exchange rate at the target, the central bank has to buy its own currency when it weakens and sell it when it strengthens, which means trading in the foreign exchange market.
